title: Think You Can Build a Game with AI? Think Again! - Danielle An & David Hoe, Meta

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 54%).

domains.label: Media & Creative
domains.rationale: The talk centers on product design qualities—taste, cohesion, aesthetics, and play-testing—that separate good AI-built games from average ones. Games are creative content and the discussion focuses on creative-production systems powered by AI tools. Coverage spans ideation via key art anchoring, development through parallel workflows, and production-scale concerns including content safety and token economics. The talk addresses creators at multiple levels but assumes basic familiarity with AI game generation, targeting intermediate practitioners. This is a conference presentation featuring interactive audience participation and live gameplay demonstrations. Speakers share direct learnings from twelve months of directing AI game-building teams at Meta with concrete worked examples.

summary: Danielle An and David Hoe from Meta's AI gaming team present a talk on building games with AI, using an interactive format where audience members scan a QR code to control NPCs that reveal slide content through a voting system. They begin by acknowledging that while many people have already built simple games using AI tools like Gemini, the novelty of prompt-generated platformers wears off quickly, and most outputs look similar. AI tools remove traditional skill barriers—coders can generate art with tools like Meta Banana or Meshy, and artists can build without engineering dependencies—but removing barriers alone does not mean everyone can make a good game. What separates good games from bad ones remains rooted in aesthetics, cohesion across UI, story, and art, real play-testing with human feedback, and ultimately taste—the feel for what subset of humans would enjoy a particular experience and why. They demonstrate a key art anchoring workflow showing how a single image can cohesively guide LLM-generated assets and gameplay. They then introduce runtime LLMs as a major new capability: NPCs driven entirely by LLMs make independent, unscripted decisions during multiplayer gameplay, enabling dynamic, non-repeatable experiences with emergent behaviors. They share three learnings from twelve months of directing AI game teams: AI enables parallel workflows replacing the linear waterfall model; runtime LLMs can personalize gameplay as a game master; and while the Star Trek vision of dynamic generation is promising, the technology alone does not automatically make better products. They further discuss Meta's platform-scale challenges: agentic systems span the entire stack from user prompting to runtime LLM decisions to content ranking and delivery, introducing non-determinism that makes stability, debugging, and scalability fundamentally harder than traditional code-based systems. Model upgrades and prompt changes can throw off entire systems, and content safety with runtime LLMs generating images and content remains a significant open challenge. They close by invoking Ready Player One's Oasis as the vision they believe is now beginning, and issue tiered calls to action: beginners should try prompting a simple game like Tetris, intermediate creators should upgrade their games with art, UI, and surprises, and advanced engineers should think about token economics, profitability, and content safety at scale.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Interactive Introduction and QR Code Demo
sections.summary: David and Danielle introduce themselves from Meta's AI team and launch an interactive experience where audience members scan a QR code to control NPCs that reveal slide content through a voting system, turning the presentation itself into a quest-giving game.

sections.title: Audience Expectations and Value Proposition
sections.summary: They set expectations: the talk is for people interested in games, how they are made, or how AI will change game development. If none of that appeals, at least attendees can play the interactive game before lunch.

sections.title: The Novelty Problem and Removed Barriers
sections.summary: They acknowledge that by 2026 many people have built simple games with AI like Gemini, but the novelty wears off and outputs look similar. AI tools remove skill barriers—coders can generate art, artists can code—but removing barriers does not mean everyone makes good games.

sections.title: Standing Out: Aesthetics, Cohesion, and Key Art Workflow
sections.summary: They explain what separates good games: aesthetics beyond simple shapes, cohesion across UI/story/art, and real play-testing. They show a video from art director Dale demonstrating how a single key art image anchors LLM-generated models, providing cohesion across art style and gameplay.

sections.title: Taste and Runtime LLM Introduction
sections.summary: They argue taste—understanding which humans will enjoy what and why—makes a game the best, not just better. They introduce runtime LLMs as living entities that modify and direct games during play, representing a new form of gameplay not possible before the last 18 months.

sections.title: Multiplayer LLM-Driven NPC Demo
sections.summary: They show a multiplayer game built in a couple days where four LLM-driven NPCs with distinct personalities independently decide to steal, block, or kick each other while competing to collect cubes—entirely unscripted, making every game unique and non-repeatable.

sections.title: Learnings from 12 Months of AI Game Building
sections.summary: They share three learnings: AI enables parallel workflows replacing the linear waterfall model, reducing iteration from months to hours; runtime LLMs can personalize gameplay as a game master; and while the Star Trek vision of dynamic generation is promising, the technology alone does not make better products, and effective use remains an active exploration area.

sections.title: Platform-Scale Challenges and Non-Determinism
sections.summary: They discuss Meta's role as a platform for millions of gaming content pieces and the challenge that agentic systems introduce non-determinism throughout the entire stack—from user prompting to runtime LLM decisions to content ranking and delivery. Model upgrades and prompt changes can throw off systems, making traditional stability, debugging, and scalability approaches inadequate.

sections.title: Ready Player One Vision and Personalization Moment
sections.summary: They invoke Ready Player One's Oasis as the vision they believe is now beginning, calling this day zero of AI transforming the gaming industry. They demonstrate a live personalization moment where an NPC (Lububu) is navigated to, illustrating how AI lets you steer any game toward anything you want.

sections.title: Tiered Call to Action and Closing
sections.summary: They issue tiered next steps: beginners should try prompting a simple game like Tetris or an infinite runner; intermediate creators should upgrade their games with art, UI, and surprises; advanced engineers should think about token economics, profitability, and content safety with runtime LLMs. They close by thanking the audience for participating with the NPCs.
